# Preface {.unnumbered}

Artificial intelligence has begun to do real work in science and engineering.
It searches spaces too large to enumerate, builds models where first principles
do not reach, proposes candidate solutions, and checks results. Can AI also
transform how we design systems and chips?

Architecture is an unusually demanding place to test that possibility. A
design decision may begin with a workload requirement and propagate through
software, interfaces, microarchitecture, RTL, and physical implementation.
Measurements are expensive and partial. A simulator, compiler, formal tool,
synthesis report, and post-layout analysis each reveal a different part of the
system, under different assumptions. Verification must establish more than
whether an artifact looks plausible, and an error discovered after fabrication
can carry far greater cost than a mistake corrected in a software release.

That difficulty is also why the opportunity is real. Architects already work
under tight power and thermal limits, with specialized components and
toolchains whose individual results must be reconciled by hand. A method that
proposes alternatives, predicts an expensive outcome, directs a scarce
experiment, or checks an artifact could improve the resulting architecture and
the cost of reaching it. It could also generate more candidates than a team can
responsibly evaluate. Faster production helps only when the rest of the design
process can still determine what those candidates mean.

I wrote this book to make that possibility concrete without assuming its
success. The moonshot behind it is an AI-assisted capability that can carry
system intent through architecture alternatives, real tools, measurements, and
verification to a technical result that an architect can defend. The ambition
is deliberately larger than generating RTL from a prompt or improving one
predictor. It asks whether the complete approach can produce a better
architecture, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or do
both. This book does not assume that the moonshot has already been achieved. It
develops the reasoning needed to pursue it without confusing progress on one
part of the problem with success as a whole.

The foundations article sets out the broad Architecture 2.0 vision
[@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. For the engineering argument in this
book, the definition below is my formulation, not a quotation from the article.

> **Architecture 2.0.** Architecture 2.0 is the practice of using AI across
> system and chip design while keeping the architecture question, current
> design state, credible alternatives, physical consequences, limits of the
> evidence, and responsibility for the decision explicit.

The architecture problem comes first. Depending on that problem, the right
approach may use generation, prediction, optimization, conventional analysis,
a combination of methods, or no AI at all. Architecture 2.0 is therefore not a
claim that every design task needs AI. It is a way to determine where AI earns
its place and what evidence its use must produce.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

This book follows an architecture question through the work required to answer
it. The architect formulates the question and represents the design state, then
chooses a method and runs the tools that can test it. What comes back has to be
interpreted, compared against a credible alternative, and turned into a
decision someone will own. That sequence keeps the book centered on what an
architect must know and do rather than on any one model or tool.

When a team claims that adopting a workflow improves an architecture design
program, the relevant object is the complete human and technical workflow.
Candidate quality, the architecture result, and the contribution of a model or
other component require separate tests. A strong model can sit inside a poor
design process. A modest method can be valuable when it removes the work that
actually limits a decision. The reader should finish the book able to do the
following work.

- Formulate the architecture question and the decision it must support.
- Diagnose which work is limiting progress before choosing a method.
- Represent the design state, relationships, permitted changes, and unknowns.
- Choose among conventional analysis, no AI, generation, prediction,
  optimization, or a small combination.
- Connect the chosen approach to real tools, reconstruct what ran, and
  determine which returns qualify as measurements.
- Compare the architecture result and the contribution of AI separately
  against credible alternatives at comparable total cost.
- Explain what the result supports, formulate a technical recommendation with
  stated limits, and identify who holds authority for commitment and who
  remains responsible.

A recurring Lighthouse case keeps these questions concrete. It begins with a
highly constrained 3\ W RISC-V subsystem for extended reality and asks what it
would take to turn a short request into a defensible system design. Nothing in
that request can be settled on its own. The power budget constrains the
accelerator, the accelerator changes the memory traffic, and the memory system
moves the thermal problem somewhere else. The book returns to this case only
when it helps expose the problem under discussion. Narrower worked material is
not presented as completion of the larger moonshot.

Three established disciplines converge here, and each overlap already has real
engineering behind it. Architecture and machine learning meet in ML for
systems, where learned models predict performance and search design spaces.
Architecture and EDA meet in chip design, where a system choice becomes RTL and
a floorplan. Machine learning and EDA meet in ML for CAD, which is already
changing synthesis, placement, routing, and verification. What this book is
after sits where all three meet.

EDA sets the hardest terms of the three. Its tools are stateful, expensive,
often dependent on proprietary inputs, and as likely to return a failure as a
measurement. A learned method that never reaches them can produce a plausible
candidate and no physical evidence at all.

![**Architecture 2.0 connects three established disciplines.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design tradeoffs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with tool-derived evidence or estimates about physical constraints. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="88%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection"}

The intersection in @fig-book-composition matters because the three overlaps
answer to different evidence. Simulator benchmarks qualify work between
architecture and machine learning, signoff and silicon qualify work between
architecture and EDA, and post-route metrics qualify work between machine
learning and EDA. Architecture 2.0 sits where all three apply at once, so
competence in one domain is not enough. A generated artifact that ignores the
workload is not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive
implementation is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair
comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

The argument also borrows discipline from outside those three. Experimental
science contributes falsifiable claims and planned tests. Statistics and
decision science help when results are noisy and an alternative still has to be
chosen. Software engineering brings versioned artifacts, regression tests, and
runs another engineer can reconstruct. Verification and systems safety keep a
returned value separate from a supported claim, and both separate from
permission to act. I draw on these practices without adopting any single discipline's
taxonomy as the book's structure.

This is not a catalog of current models, a prompt-to-chip recipe, or an
argument for using AI everywhere. It does not replace architecture judgment,
EDA, compiler engineering, or verification with a general model. Physical
checks remain central, and named people remain responsible for the question,
the interpretation, and the action taken from the result.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the computer architect. The book assumes enough
fluency to follow performance, energy, area, and software-interface tradeoffs
and to read an architecture paper, simulator report, workload study, or design
report. It does not assume a machine-learning background. The necessary ideas
are introduced through architecture problems and consequences.

Four communities come to this work from different directions, and the book is
written for what each of them already does.

- Computer architects can use the full argument to connect problem framing,
  method choice, tool execution, evidence, and commitment.
- EDA and design-automation researchers and engineers can place tools and
  measurements within the larger system decision they support.
- Machine-learning and ML-systems researchers entering architecture can see
  how data, physical constraints, evaluation cost, and verification change the
  standard for a useful result.
- Graduate students and practitioners spanning hardware and software can use
  the book to build a shared vocabulary for cross-layer design work.

These communities bring different technical strengths. The common test is
whether they can apply the reasoning to an architecture problem beyond the
recurring case and recognize when a conventional approach remains the better
choice.

## Book Structure {.unnumbered}

The foundations article establishes the broad Architecture 2.0 vision, its
history, and its capability horizons. This lecture starts from that foundation
and develops one engineering argument in three movements.

*The Moonshot and Its Motivation* defines what a complete Architecture 2.0
capability must achieve and explains why faster local automation does not
settle the larger design problem. It sets the standard used throughout the
book. A useful approach must improve the architecture, reduce the total cost
of reaching a comparable result, or do both.

*Technical Foundations* follows the information and work an architect must keep
connected. It carries the architecture question through represented design
state, method choice, real tool execution, qualified measurements, feedback,
and learning. This sequence brings a promising technique into an engineering
system instead of leaving it as an isolated result.

*Operation, Evaluation, and Responsibility* tests what survives when the
workload, software, hardware, tools, or constraints change. It evaluates the
architecture outcome, the effect of adopting the complete workflow, and the
narrower contribution of AI as separate claims. It then distinguishes the
architect's technical recommendation from the organizational authority to
commit, defer, or reject a design.

Together the three movements carry the argument from domain-level ambition to
methods an architect can apply, evaluate, and transfer to a different problem
without losing the physical and organizational limits on the result.

## How to Read This Book {.unnumbered}

Read the book sequentially the first time. Its argument accumulates. A method
choice depends on what has been represented, a measurement depends on how a
tool ran, and a recommendation depends on what the evidence can support. The
Lighthouse supplies continuity across that argument, but it remains a recurring
case rather than a universal design template.

Do not leave the reasoning attached to the examples. Apply it to another
architecture problem. Ask what decision matters, what state and constraints
must remain visible, which comparison is credible, what the tools actually
measured, and what the result still cannot establish. Transfer is the test that
the book has taught a way of thinking rather than a procedure to imitate.

Named models, benchmark scores, and tool capabilities will age, because they
capture the state of practice when this book was written. The reasoning should
outlast them. It runs from how a problem is posed and represented, through
method choice and tool discipline, to what a comparison can honestly support
and who remains responsible for acting on it. A future reader should be able to
replace every model and tool named here without losing that thread.

AI may transform system and chip design, but generation alone will not produce
that transformation. It will require design systems that connect intent to
physical evidence and architects who can judge what the evidence supports. We
can begin building that capability now. Architecture 2.0 offers a disciplined
way to decide where AI helps, where it does not, what a result means, and what
should happen next.
